newsitem.title: USA: More progress in genetics of colon cancer.
newsitem.headline: More progress in genetics of colon cancer.

text.p: Scientists on Thursday reported another advance in understanding the underlying genetics of colon cancer, a finding that could lead to better tools for early diagnosis.
Dr. Manuel Perucho and colleagues at the Burnham Institute in La Jolla, California, report their findings of a mutation in the BAX gene in Friday's edition of the journal Science.
The BAX gene is involved in cell death, a process known as apoptosis. When there is a mutation, it allows cells to proliferate and can lead to cancer.

When cells replicate, DNA repair enzymes "proofread" the genetic information in the new cells and make repairs. If there is a flaw with one of these enzymes, errors pile up and the result can be cancerous cells. This is called microsatellite mutator syndrome or "mms."
The Burnham team found that these mms cancers have a BAX mutation in their early stage of development.
Dr. John Reed, a co-author of the Science paper, said in a telephone interview that the hope is that tests for BAX mutation can be developed that will detect cancer early, before it spreads.

"Patients with a familial history of colon cancer would be candidates" for such screening, he said. If colon cancer is caught early and surgically removed, changes of survival are high. But it is hard to cure after the cancer spreads.

But Reed said more research has to be done to better understand BAX and its role. It is not yet clear whether it signals cancer, or a precancerous condition that might not warrant surgery or treatment.
"We've got to figure out whether BAX is predictive of cancer, or of a precancerous condition," he said. "We're still trying to figure out where it fits in the grand scheme of things."
